articles.title_orig: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.title_zh: ‘The Floating World’ by Ben Eastham, Reviewed
articles.content_orig:
For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, the art critic’s debut novel remains surprisingly sincere about art itself
The unnamed narrator of Ben Eastham’s debut novel, The Floating World , is, like Eastham himself , an art critic. Grieving his recently deceased wife, he feels lost while teaching at a school where the students refer to him as ‘Doctor Pissington’. Then a friend offers him a job back in the artworld. He is to work on ‘The Floating World’, which is ‘a gated community beneath a giant dome on a desert island’ being built by a tech billionaire for the wealthiest as a refuge from climate crisis and political collapse. Our morally conflicted protagonist is hired to conduct research for an art exhibition marking the island’s inauguration. The novel negotiates the contradiction of inhabiting a contemporary artworld sustained by the good intentions of art workers who align themselves with beauty and virtue, while depending on the very forces their work purports to resist.
It opens with the narrator, in Ireland, on the verge of writing, before disappearing into his recollections, and eventually returns to the point at which the story is being written (more on which later). Grief provides its emotional landscape: the narrator’s reality is shot through with the frenetic despair that comes with the sudden loss of his wife. His grief gradually becomes entangled with the project of ‘The Floating World’ and the people making it, forcing a confrontation with the loss he has been carrying. It is in such experiences that resist ordinary expression that art becomes most meaningful: a painting, for example, that is ‘a truth that didn’t need explaining. No aristocrats, no symbolism, no lies. A painting clear as love’; and another, when the narrator’s friend likens the experience of pregnancy to a painting they once saw in a museum, in which ‘The colours are stronger and brighter, there’s a texture. It’s like breaking through a screen, the world feels bigger, like it can’t be contained.’
Eastham is at his most sensitive when criticism itself becomes inadequate. There is a pleasing irony in an art critic writing about an art critic for whom, and for the artists around him, the most profound encounters with art seem to occur precisely when interpretation fails. While Eastham is tender in his descriptions of art, his acute observations of the people surrounding it can be lacerating. He has a formidable talent for summoning up a character – or skewering one – in a sentence. One woman possesses ‘the erotic hauteur of an academic who in her youth danced beneath filtered spotlights at psychedelic happenings’. Another, ‘a woman in those oversized metal-rimmed spectacles designed to signal to civilians that the wearer is an intellectual’. Eastham is exacting not only when it comes to how people appear, but also about the identities they are trying, sometimes desperately, to project. Despite the grieving anguish of its narrator, it is his wry, deadpan humour that carries the novel. There is a dryly comic sparring match with a ‘philanthropist’ who believes happiness can be quantified, and a conversation between partygoers about where, literally, ‘the shit is going’. At times it is not unlike a drawing-room comedy, with its sharp wit, back-and-forth banter and clever insults.
The metafictional frame allows the novel to avoid the aftermath of its most dramatic events, dwelling instead on the act of remembering and reconstructing them. I’m not convinced this framing adds to the reader’s understanding of the narrator’s grief or the events being recounted. The narrator returns to remarkably similar emotional terrain at the end: melancholic and still lost, but perhaps slightly more hopeful for the future. For all its suspicion of the contemporary artworld and its machinations, The Floating World remains surprisingly sincere about art itself. This is especially persuasive when Eastham uses art to give shape to experiences that elude explanation – love, pregnancy, grief – reminding us that beneath the bullshit posturing of the artworld is an unexpectedly earnest faith that art can make felt what we cannot quite articulate.
The Floating World by Ben Eastham. Fitzcarraldo Editions , £14.99 (softcover)

articles.title_orig: What the U.S.-China Board of Trade Could Mean for American Agriculture
articles.title_zh: What the U.S.-China Board of Trade Could Mean for American Agriculture
articles.content_orig:
Nevil Speer: Beef Imports Fall Short as MCOOL Debate Returns
Cattlemen’s Column: Responding to pasture mealybug
Andrew Muhammad writes in Southern Ag Today : In September 2026, the United States and China established the U.S.-China Board of Trade, creating a framework through which government officials can discuss trade issues and oversee trade initiatives between the two countries. Announced during the recent state visit by President Xi Jinping, the Board is intended to provide a regular forum for addressing trade concerns and exploring areas of mutual commercial interest (The White House, 2026). Unlike traditional trade agreements, which typically involve comprehensive negotiations and formal legislative approval, the Board functions as an executive-level arrangement through which officials can meet, exchange proposals, and consider targeted trade initiatives.
The Board’s first major initiative is the 30-for-30 Framework, announced on September 27, 2026. Under this arrangement, officials from both countries identified reciprocal lists of products representing approximately $30 billion in annual bilateral trade value on each side, with a view toward providing more favorable tariff and regulatory treatment. In simple terms, the framework seeks to expand trade in selected products rather than negotiate a broad trade agreement covering entire sectors of the economy. Whether the initiative ultimately leads to substantial increases in bilateral trade remains uncertain, but it establishes a process through which products may be considered for reduced trade barriers (Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, 2026).
How will agriculture fare under the 30-for-30 Framework? China has historically been one of the most important foreign markets for U.S. agricultural products, yet trade was significantly disrupted by the tariffs and trade tensions that emerged in recent years. U.S. agricultural exports to China approached $40 billion in 2022 but declined to approximately $8 billion by 2025 (U.S. Department of Agriculture, 2026). Given this decline, the inclusion of agricultural commodities among the products identified for possible tariff relief has attracted considerable attention.
At this stage, any assessment of the framework’s implications for agriculture is necessarily speculative. The arrangement remains a work in progress, and future tariff reductions, product coverage, and implementation details will continue to be shaped by ongoing discussions between the two countries. As a result, it is too early to determine how the framework may ultimately affect agricultural trade. Nevertheless, the product list proposed by the Chinese government may provide some initial insight into the sectors viewed as potential areas for expanded trade.
Table 1 provides a broad overview of the products included in China’s proposed import list under the 30-for-30 Framework. Based on the more than 1,600 tariff lines identified in the translated schedule (Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, 2026), the list appears to be heavily concentrated in food and agricultural products, which account for an estimated 83% of all tariff lines. Forestry products represent approximately 10%, while medical equipment, fibers, and other industrial products comprise relatively small shares. Among individual chapters, live animals, processed fruits and vegetables, wood products, oilseeds and seeds, vegetables, fish and seafood, fruits and nuts, and meats account for the largest number of tariff lines. These estimates should be interpreted with caution because the final product coverage may change. Even so, the composition of the proposed list suggests that agriculture and related sectors are likely to play a central role in any future expansion of U.S.-China trade under the framework.

articles.title_orig: USS Abraham Lincoln scheduled to dock in San Diego after harrowing stretch at sea
articles.title_zh: USS Abraham Lincoln scheduled to dock in San Diego after harrowing stretch at sea
articles.content_orig:
Deployment for nearly a year was marked by reports of supply shortages and deteriorating morale and mental health among crew
The USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been deployed for nearly a year and has spent months supporting US military operations against Iran, is scheduled to dock in San Diego on Thursday afternoon.
It marks the end of a deployment that has been described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era” and that became marked by a record-setting stretch at sea, repeated deployment extensions, and reports of supply shortages and deteriorating morale and mental health among some crew members.
The Lincoln left San Diego last November, initially bound for the Pacific. But it was redirected to the Middle East after the US and Israel launched their war with Iran in late February. The carrier remained there until late August, when it was relieved by the USS George Washington and began its journey home .
Earlier in August, the Lincoln’s deployment made headlines and faced scrutiny as reports began surfacing about poor living conditions onboard the ship, including shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. Two leading military newspapers also reported that there had been two attempts by sailors to jump overboard, causing concern among families and military health experts.
The reports prompted outrage from Democrats , while senior officials in the Trump administration pushed back . Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, called the reports “completely misrepresented ”, and when reporters asked Donald Trump if he thought the deployment had gone on too long, he responded : “Not nearly long enough” – a comment that angered some naval families.
In a statement at the time, Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command, claimed that of the US navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln had “among the lowest number of cases related to mental health”. But he said that “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect”.
Cooper said that a long deployment at sea “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways”.
Two weeks ago, as the Lincoln headed back to San Diego, Hung Cao, the acting navy secretary, acknowledged that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group attempted to take their own lives.
Sara Jacobs, a Democrat representing California’s 51st district who visited the Lincoln in late September, said in a statement last week that while she is “relieved that the USS Abraham Lincoln will soon be back in San Diego” and “looking forward to welcoming them home”, her “demand for accountability won’t end when they make port”.
“I will continue pushing for an [office of the inspector general] investigation into these conditions and a House armed services committee field hearing in San Diego to hear directly from these service members,” she said. “We need to prevent this crisis from happening ever again, and ultimately end the Iran war and bring all our service members home.”
On Wednesday, Hegseth visited the Lincoln ahead of its return, and praised the crew. He acknowledged that their deployment hasn’t been “easy”.
“When you greet your families tomorrow, just pass my gratitude from the president and myself,” Hegseth said. “Let them know that their long wait, we believe, was in service of a righteous and historic mission.”
During his remarks, Hegseth announced that those onboard the vessel would be awarded the presidential unit citation, which, according to the US military , is conferred on units of the armed forces “for extraordinary heroism in action against an armed enemy”.
Ahead of the Lincoln’s arrival on Thursday afternoon, Blue Star Families, one of the largest US-based non-profit organizations supporting active military service members, veterans and their families, said in a statement that “every homecoming is an important moment for military families”.
The organization said that it “welcomes home the sailors of USS Abraham Lincoln and wants every family to know they’re not alone as they reconnect”.
In the weeks ahead, Blue Star Families said it will host appreciation days for Lincoln sailors and their families, including several events next month in San Diego.

articles.title_orig: How Russia and the world are responding to a possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker dies
articles.title_zh: How Russia and the world are responding to a possible case of pneumonic plague after lab worker dies
articles.content_orig:

A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russia, has died just days after falling ill with an undisclosed illness.
While reports of suspected plague have been circulating in the media, Russia’s consumer health watchdog has described the illness as pneumonia of unknown cause. The World Health Organization also stated the official cause of death has not yet been confirmed. Plague therefore remains only a possible explanation.
While this is a tragic death and an important investigation, it’s certainly not a reason to panic or sign that the Black Death has returned. The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.
It’s currently not clear what the laboratory technician’s cause of death was. But as the research institute where she worked studies plague bacteria, health authorities are right to consider plague as a potential cause of illness.
The illness that she experienced – a form of pneumonia that ended in her death just a few days of contracting it – also resembles symptoms of pneumonic plague .
This form infects the lungs, usually after bacteria are inhaled and the illness can progress within a day or two. Symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath and often blood-stained sputum (mucus that is coughed up from the lungs).
But many other infections that cause pneumonia can look similar. Only laboratory tests can tell them apart. Health authorities routinely classify plague cases as suspected, probable or confirmed, so “suspected” is a normal classification at this early stage.
We don’t yet know how the laboratory worker became ill, and speculation helps no one. Early media reports of a broken sample tube have been denied by officials.
What we can say is that laboratory-acquired infections are rare but well-documented – and they tend to follow familiar patterns.
The last documented case of laboratory-acquired plague was in Chicago in 2009. As in the case in Russia, the researcher died within days of falling ill. Yersinia pestis , the bacterium that causes plague, was confirmed in his case – but investigators couldn’t establish how he became infected. It may also prove hard to establish how the laboratory worker in Russia was infected, if plague is in fact confirmed.
For respiratory pathogens, such as pneumonic plague, there are many potential routes of transmission in a lab. The main risk is inhaling tiny droplets that may be released if a tube breaks, a sample spills or a culture is handled outside normal biosafety protocols. Needle-stick injuries and splashes to the eyes are other routes.
Laboratories handling dangerous pathogens use specially designed facilities, protective equipment and strict safety protocols. While these measures help reduce the risk of accidents, it can never eliminate this risk entirely.
Authorities have identified nearly 200 people who had contact with the laboratory worker since she became unwell. They are currently under medical observation as a precaution.
Containment is a well-established protocol that is used in many infectious disease outbreaks. This involves isolating and treating cases, identifying and following up with close contacts, offering preventive antibiotics where necessary and quarantine if needed.
Monitoring contacts quickly means anyone who falls ill can be isolated and treated early. It also protects people regardless of what the cause of the illness turns out to be.
When we think about plague, we usually think of the Black Death – nightmarish plague doctors in terrifying masks and helpless medieval people covered in painful lumps ailing in bed. The Black Death killed millions globally, but today’s scenario is very different. We have access to antibiotics, laboratory tests and robust surveillance systems that make plague far less of a public health risk than it was in the medieval era.
Josephine Bourner is a Postdoctoral Research Associate in the Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry at Queen Mary University of London.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article .
Plague still thrives where people live in close contact with animals that carry fleas. Better housing, sanitation and rodent control reduce our exposure to fleas infected with plague – and therefore reduce our risk of getting bitten and contracting bubonic plague.
In places where plague occurs naturally, good hygiene and careful handling of sick, dead or hunted wild animals also lowers the risk of infection.
Bubonic plague cases are sporadic, and it rarely spreads between people. Typically, there are a few hundred cases per year worldwide, mostly in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo – though cases have been regularly reported in recent years in the United States, China, Mongolia and Peru.
Pneumonic plague is much less common. It develops when the bacteria are inhaled, or when untreated bubonic plague spreads to the lungs. It can pass from person to person, but this usually requires close contact with someone who is already unwell.
The percentage of patients who die from plague depends on whether treatment was received quickly. Untreated, bubonic plague kills an estimated 30% to 60% of patients. Untreated pneumonic plague, however, is fatal for nearly 100% of people who contract it.
Importantly, plague can be treated effectively with antibiotics that are widely available. Recent reviews have found that, if treated, only around one in six people who contract either bubonic or pneumonic plague will die from the infection.
But it’s critical that signs of plague are recognised early. Early symptoms of pneumonic plague – such as fever, headache, weakness and a cough – resemble many other illnesses. Most doctors outside endemic regions will never have seen a case, let alone suspect it. Minimising the delay between infection, suspicion and treatment is key. This is why awareness and rapid testing matter, especially for those who may have been exposed.
The risk to the public from this single suspected case in Siberia is very low, both within Russia and further afield. What matters now is whether any of those under observation fall ill, whether laboratory results confirm plague and whether investigation reveals how the laboratory worker became infected.

articles.title_orig: Genre-defying Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
articles.title_zh: Genre-defying Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
articles.content_orig:
Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.
The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
The Nobel prize, regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, is awarded for a lifetime’s body of work. The winner receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000).
Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she told Carson of the news on the phone shortly before the news broke. “She had time to tell me that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation , drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world. She has been a professor of classics at various institutions including Princeton, New York University and McGill University in Montreal. She is the 19th woman to win, out of 123 literature laureates.
Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986 and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.
Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.
In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize, for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.
David Leonard, the executive director of the Writers’ Trust of Canada , said: “Anne is such a brilliant writer. Her work is broad, but also extremely smart.” Calling Carson’s work “intoxicating”, he said her four-decade career had resulted in a peerless collection of poems and essays. “They’re beautiful, they’re smart, they’re true and they are humane. It’s exactly what we need in our writing.”
Carson’s work has attracted praise from fellow writers including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”
Anders Olsson, the chair of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel Committee for Literature, praised Carson for work that had “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”. He said: “This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.”
Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera.
Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avant-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.
In a Guardian review of Red Doc>, Sarah Crown wrote: “To engage so fluidly, so originally and compellingly, with a story first told more than 3,000 years ago, is astonishing: her ambition is one thing; the fact that it is so completely achieved is, frankly, something else.”
Much of Carson’s work has emerged from her fascination with language itself. The Swedish Academy noted: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” adding that Carson had identified the etymology of words as “the starting point for all her work”.
Asked why she continually moved between forms, Carson said in an interview: “Boredom I guess. There is a restlessness. There are a lot of forms to try.”
She has acknowledged the difficulties that come with her experimental style. “[My work] does fall apart a lot,” she said in a 2018 interview. “It gets just too weird for anyone to care about reading, or else it gets diluted into a sort of parody of itself.”
Ira Wells, the president of PEN Canada, said Carson’s win “feels particularly significant at a moment in which Canada and Europe are strengthening cultural ties amidst broader global disruption. And, on an aesthetic level, Carson’s verse vibrates on profound human frequencies, at a moment in which more and more language is formulated by machines.”
Carson has generally kept her personal life out of interviews. However, in an August 2024 article for the London Review of Books, she disclosed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.
Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.

articles.title_orig: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.title_zh: World Sight Day: Restoring sight where cataract surgery is scarce
articles.content_orig:
Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD, discusses rising cataract blindness and low-cost surgery in conflict zones for World Sight Day.
Cataract remains a leading cause of vision impairment and blindness worldwide. At least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment, and in at least 1 billion of those cases, the impairment could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cataract accounts for 94 million of those cases, and 1 in 2 people who need cataract surgery do not have access to it.¹
World Sight Day is an annual day of awareness held on the second Thursday of October and coordinated by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB). This year, it falls on October 8. The 2026 #LoveYourEyes campaign centers on personal stories, lived experiences, and community action ahead of the first Global Summit for Eye Health on November 2 in Antigua and Barbuda.²
To mark the occasion, Lloyd Williams, MD, PhD , director of Duke Global Ophthalmology at Duke Eye Center in Durham, North Carolina, spoke with Ophthalmology Times about why cataract blindness continues to rise and how teams deliver high-quality surgery in low-resource settings. Williams received the American Academy of Ophthalmology's 2025 Outstanding Humanitarian Service Award for expanding access to cataract and corneal surgery in underserved regions.
Williams attributed the increase to aging populations in regions where ophthalmic care has not expanded, compounded by conflict and poverty that make many areas harder to reach. He cited a recent cataract camp in South Sudan.
"We literally had to negotiate a ceasefire in order to do cataract surgery," Williams told Ophthalmology Times .
Williams highlighted several organizations working to expand access to eye care. Readers can donate or get involved through the following: • Duke Global Ophthalmology: Give to Duke GO .³ • Cure Blindness Project: Donate ; ophthalmologists and practices can also join its Global Partners Program.⁴ • IAPB: Individuals can become a Love Your Eyes Visionary , and organizations can apply for membership .⁵ • CBM (Christian Blind Mission): Donate .⁶ • Sightsavers: Donate or fundraise through Sightsavers USA.⁷
On a recent trip to Abyei, surgery cost approximately $70 per case using manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS), which requires a microscope as the only electrical equipment. In skilled hands, Williams said, MSICS achieves results roughly equivalent to those in the US. A $700,000 donation this year is expected to fund approximately 9000 surgeries, a volume he said would not be possible with phacoemulsification or laser-based approaches.
"I strongly believe that we're not providing somebody substandard care," Williams said.
Williams also addressed studies linking cataract surgery to lower rates of dementia diagnosis, which cannot yet establish cause and effect. He recalled veterans whose anxiety and depression appeared to improve after surgery during his residency, and he said he discusses the cognitive benefits of sight with families of older patients. Reflecting on his own vision problem as a resident, he described sight as "something that you could lose just like your arm."

articles.title_orig: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.title_zh: Webinar will commemorate World Food Day with theme “Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow”
articles.content_orig:
A webinar on 16 October will commemorate World Food Day and say farewell to the UN special rapporteur for the Right to Water and Sanitation.
The webinar will take the World Food Day theme “ Innovate today. Nourish tomorrow.” The discussion will explore what innovation can look like when we place food security, water, land, human rights, and ecological sustainability at the centre.
World Food Day is observed on 16 October each year and provides an opportunity to draw attention to hunger and food insecurity while strengthening collective action towards food systems that are sustainable, equitable, and resilient. This year ’ s webinar will bring together United Nations mandate holders, faith-based organisations, civil society organisations, and community practitioners to explore some of the challenges shaping food insecurity today – including poverty, unsustainable agricultural practices and climate change – and to share approaches that are contributing to resilience, food sovereignty, and sustainable livelihoods.
The session will also provide an opportunity to hear from Prof. Pedro Arrojo-Agudo, UN special rapporteur on the human right to safe drinking water and sanitation, whose six-year mandate concludes in November 2026.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 slides as traders monitor Treasury yields; oil gains 4%: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 slides as traders monitor Treasury yields; oil gains 4%: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 moved lower on Thursday as investors watched the moves in Treasury yields and faced pressure from elevated oil prices.
The broad market index dipped 0.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 0.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded just below the flatline.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was roughly little changed at 5.277%, as was the 30-year yield at 5.646%. The 2-year Treasury yield gained more than 3 basis points to 4.802%. Those moves came after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said more hikes may be needed to curb inflation.
Oil prices spiked also after President Donald Trump said he doesn't want to make a deal with Iran to end the war, while the U.S. is reportedly preparing for " massive bombing " in the Middle East. Brent crude jumped 4% to around $104 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures , meanwhile, advanced 4% to around $92.
Key areas of the market sensitive to higher borrowing costs such as banks and technology were under pressure yet again. Intel and Marvell Technology shares were each down more than 2%, while Bank of America and Citigroup shed around 1%.
Yields and oil have stoked volatility in equities of late, as concern grows that higher energy prices will keep inflation elevated and force the Federal Reserve to further raise rates.
Many investors are maintaining an optimistic view of the stock market, however. They expect that the start of earnings season could give the market the fuel it needs for the next leg higher.
In the third quarter, the S&P 500 is expected post a blended earnings growth rate of roughly 30%, which would be a third straight quarter of above-25% earnings growth, according to FactSet.
Palantir Technologies was one of the few stocks trading higher on Thursday, with shares gaining 4% after the name received an upgrade at Goldman Sachs . The firm called for more upside ahead as the total addressable market could be "setting up for another step function change" as a result of the shift to sovereign AI and bespoke applications.
Coffee franchise Starbucks has looked into buying restaurant chain Chipotle in a potential deal that would be the biggest restaurant acquisition of all time, the Financial Times reported on Thursday .
Chipotle's market capitalization is $39 billion, which would make a takeover more than triple the size of Burger King's $11.4bn purchase of Canadian fast food chain Tim Hortons in 2014, the paper reported.
Starbucks and Chipotle declined to comment for the story, according to the FT.
Shares of PepsiCo rose 2% in morning trading on Thursday after the company's third-quarter earnings and revenue topped analysts' expectations.
The company posted adjusted earnings of $2.34 per share on revenue of $25.27 billion, while analysts surveyed by LSEG had penciled in $2.29 in earnings per share and $24.96 billion in revenue.
With Thursday's move, the stock is heading for a winning week, as it's risen 0.3% in the period. It's down 12% on the year, however.
The three major averages fell on Thursday morning.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 181 points, or 0.4%, shortly after the opening bell. The S&P 500 shed 0.4%, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.5%.
Initial unemployment claims edged lower last week, continuing the trend of a low layoff environment, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
First-time filings for jobless benefits totaled a seasonally adjusted 197,000 for the week ended Oct. 3, down 2,000 from the prior period and just below the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 200,000.
Continuing claims, which run a week behind, rose by 17,000 to 1.72 million.
Goldman Sachs upgraded military software and analytics firm Palantir on Thursday to a buy rating from neutral.
The investment bank raised its price target on the stock to $230, implying 18.5% upside. Shares closed Wednesday at price of $194.12.
Goldman sees more government contracts, more automated workers and a more vertical supply chain in the company's future.
"The [total addressable market] may be setting up for another step function change in depth, because of the shift to sovereign AI, bespoke applications, and Palantir's newer verticalization strategy," Goldman analyst Gabriela Borges wrote in a Thursday note.
"The [forward deployed engineer] model is more than simply hiring FDEs; it requires tight feedback loops between field and product, which Palantir has perfected to the point of being able to automate via AI FDEs," she added.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise benchmark interest rates, though he isn't sure of a timetable or the degree to which it will need to happen.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal. But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur," Waller said during a speech in Turkey. "The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
In addition to his remarks on rates, the policymaker offered a defense of forward guidance, saying it can serve as an effective "signaling" tool for the Fed's expectations on where it should set rates.
Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket:
"Markets may have to climb a renewed wall of worry to set fresh records, but waiting for these concerns to fade could mean missing further gains. We believe investors should focus less on finding a perfect entry point and more on maintaining exposure while managing concentration and timing risks through a disciplined portfolio approach," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO of the Americas at UBS, said in a note.
U.S. Treasury yields climbed higher on Thursday ahead of a closely watched long-dated bond auction later.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was 4 basis points higher at 5.322%, after reaching its highest level since 2002 on Wednesday before retreating later in the day. The 30-year Treasury bond yield rose over 4 basis points to 5.705%, after trading just below a 24-year high in the previous session. The 2-year Treasury note yield was nearly 3 basis points up to 4.793%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Asia markets closed lower Thursday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 ending 1.42% lower at 69,042.11, and the broader Topix dropping 1.51% to 4,091.46.
South Korea's Kospi fell 2.62% to 6,625.93, while the small- and mid-cap Kosdaq lost 0.69% to 892.27.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.77% to 8,660.90.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down 1.43% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 1.09% lower at 4,310.28
The Governor of the Bank of France Emmanuel Moulin said Thursday that European inflation is "100%" driven by energy, adding that the geopolitical shock is now feeding into a financial shock.
As yields on French government debt surged to multiyear highs amid broader concerns over fiscal pressures in several European countries, the European Central Bank board member highlighted a "strong correlation" between oil, long-term U.S. interest rates and rates in Europe.
However, Moulin added that he does not envisage second-round effects.
Meanwhile, fellow ECB board member and president of the Dutch central bank Olaf Sleijpen said medium- to long-term inflation expectations remain "well anchored."
Stoxx 50 futures were down 0.35% ahead of Thursday's trading session, with Europe's major bourses in mixed territory prior to the market open.
The French CAC 40 was seen 0.06% lower, and Germany's DAX was down 0.27%, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 was off by 0.14%
The Italian FTSE MIB was also in negative territory, down 0.56%.
European stock markets started Thursday's session lower, with regional sectors and major bourses seen moving into negative territory in early trade.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.07% lower shortly after 8:00 a.m. in London (3:00 a.m. E.T.)

articles.title_orig: Old World Industries and Integrity Systems Form Strategic Partnership to Bring Real-Time Coolant Intelligence to AI Data Centers
articles.title_zh: Old World Industries and Integrity Systems Form Strategic Partnership to Bring Real-Time Coolant Intelligence to AI Data Centers
articles.content_orig:
NORTHBROOK, Ill. and WEATHERFORD, Texas, Oct. 8, 2026
Thermal Charge® Heat Transfer Fluids and AI-Powered Monitoring Unite to Deliver Predictive Cooling-Loop Health Management
NORTHBROOK, Ill. and WEATHERFORD, Texas , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Old World Industries (OWI), a leading manufacturer of coolant and heat transfer solutions best known for its brands of PEAK® and Thermal Charge® Heat Transfer Fluids, and Integrity Systems, a critical infrastructure monitoring company, today announced a strategic partnership to combine coolant expertise with real-time monitoring, predictive analytics and intelligent diagnostics for data center cooling systems.
As AI and other high-density computing workloads place increasing demands on data center infrastructure, operators need greater visibility into the real-time health and performance of their cooling systems. Any downtime or disruptions to the system can have significant operational and financial consequences, making proactive monitoring and maintenance critical for data center operators. Periodic laboratory testing provides important point-in-time information about coolant condition; the OWI-Integrity Systems partnership is designed to complement that testing with continuous field monitoring that can alert operators of changing cooling-loop conditions between testing intervals.
"Unscheduled downtime remains one of the most expensive risks facing data center operators today," said Greg Noethlich, Chief Executive Officer of OWI. "This partnership helps customers move from reactive problem-solving to predictive maintenance, helping avoid the substantial costs associated with unexpected system failures."
Integrity Systems' real-time industrial monitoring, predictive analytics and intelligent diagnostics capabilities are designed to work alongside existing controls and monitoring systems. Its platform brings together sensor data, operating context, maintenance history and operator knowledge to help identify developing problems and guide maintenance decisions.
"We founded Integrity Systems to close the gap between what industrial operators need and what predictive monitoring actually delivers," said Brett Wade, Chief Executive Officer of Integrity Systems. "By combining continuous field monitoring with OWI's coolant expertise, the partnership delivers ongoing visibility into coolant performance, helping operators make informed maintenance decisions based on real-time operating conditions."
The collaboration also creates an opportunity to generate additional real-world operating data on coolant performance. Those insights can help inform future product validation and development while giving operators greater context about cooling system conditions in live environments.
"We see AI's future being shaped not only by the size of the data centers behind it, but by the ability to deploy increasing levels of intelligence at the edge," said Connor Wooley, Chief Technology Officer of Integrity Systems. "Our goal is to lead in that space by delivering AI where work is performed and critical decisions are made. Our agentic harness is designed to turn deep analysis and verified operating experience into specialized AI that runs locally. With OWI, we're applying that approach to coolant and cooling-system health, helping operators understand what is changing, why it matters, and when to act. But our vision extends further, an operating system for intelligent infrastructure that can carry that capability beyond continuous human reach, from remote industrial environments to space. The goal is intelligence that can operate where people cannot always be, without depending on a distant data center for every decision."
Together, OWI and Integrity Systems are enabling a new standard for cooling-system assurance that helps data center operators improve uptime, protect critical infrastructure and confidently scale for growing computing demands. To learn more about the partnership, visit thermalcharge.com or integrityus.ai.
Contact information: Old World Industries Dylan Tosti, Assistant Marketing Manager, Brand Marketing dtosti@owi.com
Integrity Systems Brett Wade, Chief Executive Officer brettwade@integrityus.ai
About Old World Industries Old World Industries is among the largest privately held companies competing in the automotive aftermarket. The Northbrook, Illinois-based company has a presence in various consumer product markets worldwide. Old World's brands include a full line of PEAK® Automotive Aftermarket Products, including Antifreeze & Coolant, Washer Fluid, Lighting and Wiper Blades; BlueDEF® Diesel Exhaust Fluid and Equipment; FINAL CHARGE® PRO-SERIES Heavy Duty Extended Life Coolant; THERMAL CHARGE® Heat Transfer Fluids; and Fleet Charge® SCA Precharged Heavy Duty Coolant. For more information, please visit owi.com.
About Integrity Systems Integrity Systems is building an operating system for industrial and critical infrastructure. Its platform brings together sensor data, operating context, maintenance history, and operator knowledge to help identify root causes, anticipate developing problems, and guide maintenance decisions. Designed to work alongside existing controls and monitoring systems, Integrity's agentic harness connects deeper analysis with specialized intelligence that can run locally, close to the equipment. Its approach grounds recommendations in traceable evidence and uses verified operating outcomes to improve future insights. For more information, please visit integrityus.ai.

articles.title_orig: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.title_zh: New GETI publication explores future of Christian unity
articles.content_orig:
A new publication from the World Council of Churches (WCC) Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation (EEF) brings together the voices and theological reflections of young ecumenists from around the world who attended the 2025 edition of the WCC Global Ecumenical Theological Institute (GETI). It brings fresh inputs to the pressing question for the churches today: Where now for visible unity?
From left: Rev. Prof. Dr Meehyun Chung, moderator of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi, WCC programme executive for Ecumenical Theological Education and coordinator of GETI 2025; Rev. Dr Nathan Digby, GETI 2025 facilitator and member of the WCC Commission on Ecumenical Education and Formation; during the launch event of the GETI 2025 book on 8 October.
“ GETI 2025: Voices and Visions of Transformative Unity,” edited by Prof. Dr Ani Ghazaryan Drissi and Rev. Prof. Teddy Chalwe Sakupapa, emerges from the WCC ’ s 4th GETI, held in the context of the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order in Wadi El Natrun, Egypt. The publication, launched on 8 October, during the biannual meeting of the EEF Commission, comes at a significant moment.
“ The fruits of ecumenical dialogue must take root in the lives of our churches,” said Drissi. “ The GETI 2025 message brought this bold challenge to the Sixth World Conference on Faith and Order and the wider ecumenical movement: let the unity we confess become the life we share.”
This publication carries that call forward, she added, through voices and visions rooted in different churches, cultures, and lived realities. “ Their theological reflections invite us to ask how the fruits of ecumenical dialogue can shape our communities, deepen our relationships, and renew our common witness,” said Drissi. “ They call us to listen more deeply, confront exclusion, and share responsibility for the future of our churches.”
Bossey students who took part of GETI 2025 shared their testimonies during the launch event.
The volume presents a global and contextually grounded exploration of Christian unity. Its contributors reflect on reception, Nicaea, pilgrimage, trust and companionship, while also addressing colonial wounds, trauma, migration, ethnic violence, Palestine, digital ecumenism, and ecological crisis.
Rather than treating unity as an abstract theological ideal, the book emphasizes unity as something that must be embodied through relationships, truth-telling, healing, solidarity, and public witness. Its concluding message describes young ecumenists as contributors to the present and future of the ecumenical movement.
GETI 2025 facilitator and EEF commissioner Rev. Dr Nathan Digby explained that a central goal of the WCC ’ s Ecumenical Theological Education work is to provide opportunities for emerging ecumenical leaders to be formed in ecumenism and to ensure that their voices are heard, encouraged, and shared with the wider church.
“ The publication of GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity gives concrete expression to this commitment,” he said. “ As part of their theological formation, students participating in GETI 2025 developed academic papers exploring the theme of visible Christian unity in relation to their own theological interests, contexts, and experiences.”
This volume recognizes and celebrates their intellectual and theological work while creating a platform through which their perspectives can contribute to broader conversations about the future of Christian unity, added Digby.
“ By bringing these emerging voices together in one publication, GETI 2025: Voices and Visions for Transformative Unity not only documents an important dimension of the GETI experience but also invests in the next generation of ecumenical thinkers and leaders, whose insights and visions are essential for shaping a more transformative and visible unity among Christians.”
Published by WCC Publications, the book offers churches, theological institutions, students, and ecumenical partners a rich resource for reflection and conversation on the future of Christian unity.
The session also included the presentation of the GETI Visual Report and a short video featuring voices and moments of GETI 2025.
The EEF Commission is meeting at the WCC Ecumenical Institute at Bossey 4-9 October.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.content_orig:
⛈️🌊 Track the storm, check your local risk and get more detailed timing from meteorologists in the CNN Weather app
The sun has come up to reveal Hurricane Isaias and its swirling clouds above the Gulf’s record-warm water.
True color satellite imagery shows us what a storm looks like with the naked eye from space — think of it as what you’d see if you were on the space station.
But you need sunlight to illuminate the clouds and use this imagery. The storm’s bright white clouds appear in the loop as the satellite captures the moment of this morning’s sunrise.
Here’s a look at Isaias’ impacts and when to expect them in cities along the Gulf Coast.
For those who lived through Helene, another hurricane bringing rain to the mountains may stir understandable anxiety. But Isaias’ forecast points to a more limited flood threat.
Parts of the southern Appalachians could see 3 to 5 inches Saturday, with locally significant flooding possible.
During Helene, some mountain areas received up to 10 inches before the hurricane arrived. Moisture streaming ahead of Helene fueled a separate area of persistent downpours, known as a “predecessor rain event,” or PRE.
The hurricane then dumped torrential rain onto saturated ground, with mountain slopes enhancing the rainfall. The combined multiday event piled up 20 to 30 inches of rain in some parts of western North Carolina.
Isaias’ quick movement should help limit rainfall totals, though locally higher amounts remain possible. Residents should keep watching for forecast changes as the storm draws closer.
Isaias is forecast to run into some storm-disrupting wind shear the closer it gets to the US coast. This shear — changes in wind speed or direction at different levels of the atmosphere — is going to push Isaias a little off-kilter, focusing the worst of its wind and rain on the north side of the storm.
This lopsidedness will weaken Isaias — but also expand the reach of its winds.
A stronger storm tends to stay compact, like an ice skater spinning. Try to knock that same skater off balance, they’ll put out their arms to steady themself.
That’s basically the same thing we’re expecting with Isaias’ winds — instead of staying confined closer to the center, they’ll stretch out farther. More places could be hit with Isaias’ strong winds as a result, even if the storm is a bit weaker overall.
If Isaias makes landfall as a hurricane, it will mark the first hurricane landfall anywhere in the United States in two years.
No hurricane has come ashore in the US since 2024’s Hurricane Milton . Milton slammed into Florida’s Gulf Coast as a Category 3 major hurricane on October 9, 2024.
Isaias is forecast to weaken, but still remain a formidable storm before landfall Friday night or very early Saturday morning. It could come ashore as a Category 1 or a lower-end Category 2 hurricane before quickly becoming a tropical storm after landfall.
Regardless of its strength, Isaias will be the fourth named storm to make landfall in the US this season. The three others have been short-lived tropical storms: Arthur impacted Texas on June 17; Bertha hit Louisiana on July 22; and Edouard made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border on September 1.
All Mobile County and Baldwin County Public schools in Alabama will be closed on Friday as Hurricane Isaias is expected to impact the northern Gulf Coast this weekend.
“We do not like to do this, because it affects so many, but we have to take all factors into consideration and of course, the most important, the safety of our students and our staff,” Baldwin County Public Schools Superintendent Marty McRae said announcing the closure on Wednesday .
All of Baldwin County Public Schools’ afterschool and extracurricular activities scheduled for Friday and Saturday are also canceled.
“I cannot risk anyone’s safety,” Mobile County Public Schools Superintendent Chresal Threadgill said in his closure announcement . “The weather conditions currently remain extremely unpredictable.”
Isaias remains a Category 1 hurricane with sustained winds of 80 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center’s 7 a.m. CT update.
The hurricane has maintained its strength over the past few hours but is still set to strengthen today. It’s forecast to peak as a high-end Category 2 hurricane sometime Thursday night.
A Hurricane Hunter aircraft is currently flying into Isaias, so we’ll get a more precise measurement of its current strength soon.
At least 14 Florida Panhandle counties are closing public schools Friday, and many have closed Thursday, according to the state’s Department of Education.
Florida State University’s campus in Panama City is also closed.
The right side of a hurricane, relative to its forward motion, typically packs the most extreme conditions, and it’s all because of their counterclockwise rotation.
Wind speeds are amplified because the rotation pushes air in the same direction as the storm is moving. The area with the most extreme winds and intense storms sits just to the right of a hurricane’s eye, in the eye wall.
Because of boosted winds, tornadoes also occur more frequently on the right side. Faster winds increase areas of wind shear — a change in wind speed or direction with height — which tornadoes need to spin up.
Similarly, surge is also enhanced. As storms approach land, wind piles up and pushes seawater towards the coast on the right side of a hurricane. On the left side of a hurricane, wind does the opposite and can actually drain bays.
This will all be true for Isaias but may be even more so because it’s expected to become lopsided as it battles wind shear near the Gulf Coast. More thunderstorms and rain will likely be concentrated on the hurricane’s eastern half.
Isaias is guaranteed to knock out power and down trees where it makes landfall along the coast, but outages could extend further inland into parts of the Southeast.
Isaias will be moving fast and grow larger before it moves inland. Those are two of the factors that will fuel wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph that will spread northward into parts of central and northern Alabama, northern Georgia and northeast Mississippi on Saturday.
Those gusts are nowhere near as fierce as what the coast will see, but it could be enough to cause at least isolated to scattered power outages, particularly in Alabama.
As Tropical Storm Isaias heads towards the Gulf Coast, many residents began preparing days in advance.
Residents flocked to grocery stores and gas stations in Pensacola, Florida to stock up in preparation causing long lines at some locations.
As Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast, all eyes are on how it will impact one of the biggest games of the college football season.
The storm could make landfall Saturday, hours before No. 2 Georgia plays No. 6 Alabama in Tuscaloosa in a game that President Donald Trump is planning to attend.
While the storm could prompt other schools in the region to cancel games, change kickoff times, or even move games to other locations, Alabama said “there are no plans to alter the contest” in a statement Wednesday evening.
When asked whether the storm will change his travel plans to Alabama, Trump said, “We’ll have to see.”
Team officials offered few details on contingency plans if the storm were to intensify.
Even if the game goes on as planned, meteorologists predict players and spectators may feel some effects of the storm.
Heavy rain and gusty winds could make for a soggy, blustery Saturday evening in Tuscaloosa.
A faster-moving storm could allow conditions to improve before or during the game, but that’s not the most likely outcome right now. The timing will be key.
When Isaias rapidly intensified into a hurricane last night, it was undergoing a phenomenon that is becoming more common as the planet heats up.

articles.title_orig: More physical activity may mean slower Parkinson’s disease progression
articles.title_zh: More physical activity may mean slower Parkinson’s disease progression
articles.content_orig:
Higher levels of physical activity were associated with slower cognitive decline and motor progression in mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease (PD) over up to 7 years of follow-up, a longitudinal cohort study showed.
While the greatest cognitive benefits were observed in patients who reported more than 8 hours of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per week, those who were active for at least 4 hours a week also showed slower decline than individuals who were less active. The same held true for motor progression, with all levels of activity showing some benefit but those getting more exercise reporting the slowest motor decline.
In additional analyses, vigorous activity showed no association with either outcome beyond that of total activity time. Recent activity remained associated with both outcomes after adjustment for activity in the 10 years before enrollment.
The data add to limited evidence on the relationship between physical activity and cognitive decline in PD and offer a longer-term picture of protective motor benefits that that short-duration trials were could not provide.
"Our findings suggest that physical activity may influence the cognitive trajectory of Parkinson's disease, alongside its motor benefits," senior investigator Alberto J. Espay, MD, MSc, a movement disorders specialist and professor of neurology at the University of Cincinnati, told Medscape Medical News .
"That is encouraging, but it does not establish that exercise prevents cognitive decline or dementia," Espay said, adding that randomized evidence is still needed, along with confirmation that the differences translate into preserved everyday function.
The study was published online October 7 in Neurology .
No drug has been proven to modify the course of PD. Exercise has been studied as one possible way to do so, and two randomized trials have shown short-term motor benefits.
In Park-in-Shape , 130 patients with early PD who completed 6 months of home-based aerobic exercise had a smaller increase in off-medication motor scores than an active control group.
In the phase 2 SPARX trial , 6 months of high-intensity treadmill exercise was associated with less motor worsening than usual care, whereas moderate-intensity exercise did not differ from usual care.
As reported previously by Medscape Medical News , a 2022 study in Neurology linked regular moderate-to-vigorous exercise in early PD with slower decline in processing speed.
But testing long-term effects in randomized trials is difficult because restricting physical activity in a control group for years is neither ethical nor practical, the investigators of the 2022 study wrote. Adherence problems and crossover between groups can also erode the difference in exposure over time.
To address the lack of long-term data, the current study's investigators analyzed data from 294 patients with mild-to-moderate PD (mean age, 66.4 years; 33% women) enrolled in the Cincinnati Cohort Biomarker Program between January 2019 and February 2025.
Clinical research fellows gave patients a structured interview, adapted from a questionnaire used in other large PD cohorts, that recorded weekly hours of moderate and vigorous activity at work, at home, and during recreation.
Moderate activities included brisk walking, nonstrenuous bicycling, doubles tennis, light swimming, and household chores. Vigorous activity included such activities as jogging, fast bicycling, aerobics, or snow shoveling.
Patients were divided into tertiles of total weekly activity: up to 4 hours, 4-8 hours, and more than 8 hours. Baseline Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and motor scores did not differ significantly across groups, although the most active patients were younger. Patients were followed for cognitive function for up to 5 years and up to 7 years for motor function (median follow-up for both, 3 years).
Motor scores were assessed while patients were in the "on" state, when their usual PD medication was taking effect.
In models adjusted for age, sex, disease duration, education, BMI, and baseline disease stage, each additional weekly hour of activity was associated with 0.035 fewer points in MoCA decline per year ( P < .001) and 0.082 fewer points in motor worsening per year ( P = .020).
The middle tertile also declined more slowly on the MoCA than the least active group ( P = .005), with no significant differences between the middle and highest tertile groups.
The cognitive association held after investigators excluded four participants in the least active group who declined unusually fast, whereas the motor association weakened.
On the motor examination section of the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS-III), where higher scores indicate worse function, the average score at baseline was 23. Scores rose by 0.143 points per year in the least active group but fell by 0.783 points per year in the most active group.
The highest activity group reported significantly slower MDS-UPDRS-III progression than those who were physically active for fewer than 4 hours a week ( P = .048).
"Taken together, these results suggest that physical activity may provide dual clinical benefits by independently reducing both motor progression and cognitive decline in PD," researchers wrote. "Furthermore, the observed effects of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity were more strongly related to activity duration than intensity and were not explained by baseline activity level."
Study limitations include the observational design, self-reported activity, and a single-center cohort that was 98.3% White. Patients excluded from the analysis, most often for missing activity data, were older and had higher baseline motor scores than those included.
While previous studies have demonstrated the potential short-term neuroprotective benefits of exercise, researchers say the new findings fill a gap in the literature on long-term effects. But the question of how physical activity is linked to cognitive and motor function preservation remains unanswered.
"I suspect several pathways work together, rather than one mechanism explaining both findings," Espay said. "Improved blood flow, reduced inflammation, and greater capacity for synaptic adaptation could support the brain networks involved in both movement and cognition."
The range of biological effects is what makes exercise a compelling candidate for disease modification, said Bastiaan R. Bloem, MD, PhD, professor of neurology and director of the Center of Expertise for Parkinson and Movement Disorders at Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen, Netherlands. Bloem led the Park-in-Shape trial but was not involved in the new study.
"It has anti-inflammatory components. It enhances blood flow. It increases neurotrophic factors. It drives neuroplasticity," he said.
Bloem's group found in a follow-up imaging analysis of Park-in-Shape that patients who exercised built new functional connectivity in the brain and had less brain atrophy than a stretching control group. The new study's greatest strength is its long follow-up, since randomized trials have often been limited to months, he said.
But Espay said that whether those biological pathways explain the associations seen in the Cincinnati cohort is not yet clear.
"We cannot establish the direction of causation from these data, and the relationship may run both ways," he said, adding that people with slower progression may be better able to stay active. Only a clinical trial can settle the question, he added.
The investigators wrote that examining the relationship between physical activity and disease-related biomarkers — including alpha-synuclein, amyloid-beta, and tau in cerebrospinal fluid — could help clarify whether the benefits are disease-specific. That analysis is planned but has not yet begun, Espay said.
Daniel M. Corcos, PhD, studies exercise in PD in the Department of Physical Therapy and Human Movement Sciences at Northwestern University,

articles.title_orig: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.title_zh: Amoris laetitia: Pastoral experiences in Asia and challenges of digital world
articles.content_orig:
Families today are âa challenging mosaic of diverse realities, marked by joys, hopes, struggles and wounds. The family is not only a place to which the Church brings the Gospel. It is also a place from which the Gospel comes alive â from one generation to another, from one family to another, and from families to society.â
Cardinal Filipe Neri Ferrão, Metropolitan Archbishop of Goa and Daman, opened his address with this reflection at the start of the second day of Pope Leo XIVâs meeting with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Bishopsâ Conferences, ten years after Amoris laetitia .
The Indian Cardinal addressed the theme âFamilies today: reality, beauty and challenges. Discerning the signs of the times through the experience of families and the Churchâs pastoral commitment today.â
He invited participants in the meeting, conducted in a synodal style, to ask themselves in their discernment: âWhat is the Holy Spirit asking the Church to change?â
This concerned ânot only in what we do for the families, but in how we understand, accompany and empower them as protagonists of the Gospel and as enduring loci of Godâs revelation.â
Drawing on his experience as a pastor in Asia, particularly in India, Cardinal Neri Ferrão acknowledged that families had changed in their identity, nature, and composition, with smaller households, new forms of cohabitation, and interreligious marriages.
Families were increasingly on the move, and many faced economic insecurity, poverty, unemployment, and uncertainty about the future.
âChristian families in many parts of India and Asia,â the Cardinal stressed, âmust also live amid growing religious polarisation and hostility, making the public expression and transmission of faith increasingly difficult.â
Yet, these families also offered the Church beauty through their care for children, the elderly, the sick, and vulnerable people. Even amid poverty and uncertainty, the Cardinal explained, âour families continue to create positive spaces for joy and hope.â
Following the publication of Amoris laetitia , he recalled, the Churches in India and across Asia âlistened first to families,â and that listening âshaped how we walk with them. We now see marriage preparation as the start of a lifelong journey, offer spiritual renewal and counselling to couples and children, and keep forming families and lay leaders over time.â
He stressed that pastoral ministry needed to move âfrom mission to families to mission among families.â Families were not simply recipients of assistance but, in his words, âthe Church's partners in mission.â
Cardinal Neri Ferrão concluded by recounting the experience of a priest who had begun family ministry in his parish not with a program, but by visiting a family experiencing underlying difficulties in communication between the parents and between them and their children. It had begun with âa conversation and a willingness to listen.â
The second speaker, Vincenzo Rosito, Professor of the History and Culture of Family Institutions at the Pontifical Lateran University and Vice Dean of the Pontifical John Paul II Theological Institute for Marriage and Family Sciences, summed up his address with questions to guide participantsâ synodal discernment.
He began with an invitation inspired by Pope Leo XIVâs reflections in the encyclical Magnifica humanitas : âLet each of us be mindful of the relationships we build within our own families and within the Church.â
Professor Rosito stressed that âfamily practices, in fact, help us to understand how churches and families learn from one another. Both the Church and the family, in fact, learn through the practices of their daily lives.â
He then offered a question for participants to consider as a father, mother, theologian, or pastor: âAm I able to recognise and share with others at least one new thing that I have learnt to do, or to do differently, in recent years of my family or pastoral life?â
Changes in family life, Prof. Rosito explained, âare not problemsâ but âhuman activities.â Recalling Amoris laetitia , he presented them as an opportunity, as concrete processes âin which individuals and families act, react, learn and develop new resources.â
âConsider, for example,â the political philosopher continued, âhow the use of new digital technologies is transforming the daily habits of families and the way children are brought up.â
The family and the Church, Prof. Rosito continued, âlearn together through change.â He drew on the Gospel image of Jesus, Joseph, and Maryâs flight into Egypt.
He noted that today, âdrawing on the experiences of refugee and migrant families, some Christian communities are re-establishing themselves as ârefuge churchesââ for those arriving in a new land or making a long journey.
He also addressed the tragedy of violence shared by many families: âThe insecurity stemming from social and political violence is a worrying reality that many Churches must deal with today, in their daily lives.â Such insecurity, he warned, could âeven devour family bonds and church relationships themselves.â
Josephâs dream was also part of the experience of this flight.
âTo dream, to imagine new forms for the Church,â Prof. Rosito concluded, âalso means renewing what we already do. To imagine the Church means being willing to learn from one another, whilst we are transformed together, as churches and as families.â
His final question for discernment was therefore: âWhat do we need, amidst the light and shadow of today, to learn and imagine new ways of being a family and new ways of being the Church?â

articles.title_orig: France Is Veering Toward a Potential Debt Crisis, a Warning to the World
articles.title_zh: France Is Veering Toward a Potential Debt Crisis, a Warning to the World
articles.content_orig:
France has been engulfed by turmoil, with students out on the streets to protest cuts at schools. Investors are rebelling against the government, too, by questioning the country’s ability to manage its huge debt pile.
France has emerged as the European epicenter of global turmoil in bond markets and serves as a warning to politicians around the world contending with higher borrowing costs. It’s a perilous financial backdrop to the protests. On Thursday, for the second time in a week , high school students and their supporters came out across France, calling for more teachers and the renovation of dilapidated school buildings.
Rising interest rates expose the vulnerability of countries with high debt burdens and stubborn deficits. When governments must spend more on debt payments, it leaves less money for other priorities like improving schools, building more housing or cutting taxes — and that can push frustrated voters into the streets or into the arms of populist political parties.
“These bond yield rises have very real implications,” said Mahmood Pradhan, a nonresident fellow at Bruegel, a think tank in Brussels, and former deputy director of the European department at the International Monetary Fund.
In a nightmare scenario, the dynamics become a self-fulfilling spiral: Politicians make more promises to appease aggrieved citizens, leading to more borrowing and, in turn, spooking investors, who demand even higher rates to keep buying government bonds.
France shows how quickly the situation can escalate when investor sentiment turns sour.

articles.title_orig: NASA photo of Mars dawn reveals cliffs in unprecedented detail
articles.title_zh: NASA photo of Mars dawn reveals cliffs in unprecedented detail
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.
Curiosity was built by NASA JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. NASA JPL leads the mission on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of its Mars Exploration Program portfolio. Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego built and operates Mastcam.
